intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13), of which this is the twelfth chapter of the text and the second-last of the carita. In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahāsarasvatī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 5), not a statement of the Purāṇa text. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 12 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna, of Durgā: radiant as a garland of lightning, seated on the shoulder of the lion, terrible, attended by maidens with sword and shield in hand, holding in her hands the discus, mace, sword, shield, arrows, bow, bowstring (गुणम्) and the threatening gesture (तर्जनीम्), fiery in nature, bearing the moon, three-eyed. The dhyāna is liturgy; the chapter itself names Caṇḍikā, Mahākālī, Lakṣmī and Alakṣmī, not Durgā.
intro.summary: The Devī, still before the gods who have just praised her, speaks (12.1). Whoever praises her daily with these hymns, with a collected mind, she will rid of every affliction (12.2). Those who recite the three stories — Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣa, Śumbha and Niśumbha (12.3) — or hear her Māhātmya with devotion on the eighth, fourteenth and ninth lunar days (12.4) will know no sin, no misfortune born of sin, no poverty, no parting from those they love (12.5), and no fear of enemies, robbers, the king, weapons, fire or flood (12.6). The text is therefore to be recited and heard: it is the highest svastyayana (12.7). It quells the calamities of pestilence and the threefold portent (12.8); where it is rightly recited every day in her shrine she will never leave (12.9). It is to be recited at offerings, worship, the fire rite and festivals (12.10), and she accepts worship done with knowledge or without it (12.11). Heard at the great yearly worship of autumn, it frees a man from every trouble and gives him wealth, grain and sons (12.12–13); it makes him fearless, destroys his enemies and makes his family flourish (12.14–15). It is to be heard at rites of pacification, after evil dreams and under planetary affliction, and turns the evil dream into a good one (12.16–17); it brings peace to children seized by bālagrahas and reconciles men who have fallen apart (12.18), breaks the power of the wicked and, by its recitation alone, destroys rākṣasas, bhūtas and piśācas (12.19). The whole Māhātmya makes her present (12.20); the delight a year of offerings gives her — animals, flowers, arghya, incense, perfume, lamps, feeding of brāhmaṇas, homa, sprinklings and gifts — one hearing of this story gives her too, and, heard, it takes away sins and grants health (12.20–22). The telling of her births protects from evil beings, the story of her battles removes the fear of enemies, and the hymns of the gods, of the brahmarṣis and of Brahmā grant an auspicious mind (12.23–25). In a forest fire, among robbers or enemies, pursued by beasts, condemned by a king, in chains, in a storm at sea, in battle or in pain, the one who remembers her story is set free; beasts, robbers and enemies flee from him from afar (12.25–30). The seer resumes (12.31): Caṇḍikā vanishes as the gods watch (12.32–33); the gods take up their offices and their shares of the sacrifice again (12.33–34), and, with Śumbha and Niśumbha slain, the Daityas who are left go down to Pātāla (12.34–35). Medhas then gives King Suratha the lesson: eternal as she is, the Goddess comes forth again and again to protect the world (12.36); she deludes the universe and gives it birth, and grants knowledge when entreated and prosperity when pleased (12.37); the cosmic egg is pervaded by her as Mahākālī, who at the great time takes the form of Mahāmārī (12.38); she is dissolution, creation and preservation (12.39), Lakṣmī in good times and Alakṣmī in decline (12.40); and, praised and worshipped, she gives wealth, sons, a mind set on dharma and a good destiny (12.41).
intro.forms: The Devī, speaking in the first person through the whole phalaśruti (12.1–30): the one who destroys affliction (12.2), who abides where her text is recited (12.9, 12.20), and who accepts worship with love (12.11, 12.22). In the narrator’s voice she is the Blessed Caṇḍikā, fierce in valour (भगवती चण्डिका चण्डविक्रमा, 12.32), and the Blessed Goddess, eternal and still arising again and again (भगवती देवी … नित्या अपि पुनः पुनः सम्भूय, 12.36). Medhas’s closing verses name her powers: she who deludes the universe and brings it forth (12.37); Mahākālī, whose form at the great time is Mahāmārī, the great Death (12.38; the same word names the pestilence in 12.8); the unborn (अजा) and the eternal (सनातनी), who is creation and preservation as well as dissolution (12.39); Lakṣmī, giver of increase, and Alakṣmī, for ruin (12.40). Her ‘births’ (जन्मनाम्, 12.23) and ‘auspicious manifestations’ (उत्पत्तयः शुभाः, 12.14) are her appearances in the three stories. Mahākālī here is a name used in its own sense, not the liturgical presiding form of the first carita.
intro.significance: The chapter takes its name from its content (colophon: फलस्तुतिः). Its distinction is that the phalaśruti is spoken by the Devī herself, not by a narrator or a later editor: in her own voice she names the three stories (12.3), the days (12.4, 12.12), the occasions (12.10, 12.16) and the fruits of reciting, hearing and remembering them. It thus defines the text as a practice and lays the foundation on which the Saptaśatī is used in Śākta worship — daily pāṭha, the autumn Navarātra, rites of pacification. The narrative then closes the third story: the gods regain their offices and their shares of the sacrifice (12.33–34), and the surviving Daityas go to Pātāla (12.35), the terms the Devī sent to Śumbha in 8.26. Finally Medhas turns back to the king and restates the teaching he began with in chapter 1 — the Goddess deludes the world and gives it birth (12.37, as 1.55–56), and is eternal though she ‘arises’ (12.36, as 1.64–66) — so that the three stories stand between two statements of the same doctrine. Chapter 13 returns to Suratha and the merchant.
intro.grammar: A first-person speech of promise, and so a chapter of futures: स्तोष्यते, नाशयिष्यामि (12.2), कीर्तयिष्यन्ति (12.3), श्रोष्यन्ति (12.4), भविष्यति (12.5, 12.13), सम्भविष्यति (12.6), विमोक्ष्यामि (12.9) and the epic future प्रतीच्छिष्यामि (12.11), mostly in relative–correlative sentences (यः … तस्य, 12.2; ये … तेषाम्, 12.3–5; या … सा, 12.21–22). Gerundives command the practice (पठितव्यम्, श्रोतव्यम्, with an instrumental agent, 12.7; उच्चार्यम्, श्राव्यम्, 12.10) and optatives prescribe it or state its power (शमयेत्, 12.8; शृणुयात्, 12.16; मुच्येत, 12.29). Passives (पठ्यते, 12.9; क्रियते, 12.12, 12.22; मोह्यते, 12.37), locatives of occasion (12.4, 12.10, 12.16), locative absolutes (सुचरिते श्रुते, 12.22; तस्मिन् श्रुते, 12.24; पतत्सु शस्त्रेषु, 12.28; शुम्भे निहते, 12.34–35) and ablatives in -तः (शत्रुतः, दस्युतः, राजतः, 12.6) are frequent. Taddhita abstracts (दारिद्र्यम्, 12.5; सांनिध्यम्, 12.9; आरोग्यम्, 12.22) and agent compounds (शान्तिकारकम्, 12.18; बलहानिकरम्, 12.19; सन्निधिकारकम्, 12.20) describe the text’s effects. The learner also meets epic forms (नन्दते, 12.15; the neuter दुःस्वप्नम्, 12.17; the nominative उत्पत्तयः after श्रुत्वा, 12.14), the irregular stems पुंस् (पुमान्, 12.14; पुंसाम्, 12.15, 12.24) and नृ (नृभिः, नृणाम्), and, in the closing narrative, the imperfect अन्तरधीयत (12.33), the perfects चक्रुः and आययुः (12.34–35) and the absolutive सम्भूय (12.36).
intro.teaching: Literally, the chapter is a list of promises: recite, hear or remember this text, and sin, poverty, fear, disease, evil dreams and danger will leave you; then the Goddess vanishes, the gods return to their places, and Medhas tells the king what she is. The traditional uses of the chapter — the Navarātra pāṭha (12.4, 12.12), the recitation within every rite and the caṇḍī-homa (12.10), 12.13 recited as a sampuṭa — are the tradition’s, and the commentary presents them as such. As teaching, the chapter shifts the weight of worship from the rite to attention: she accepts what is offered in ignorance (12.11); one hearing equals a year of offerings (12.22); and in danger, where no rite can be performed, what saves is remembering (स्मरन्, 12.29). Medhas’s close joins this to the doctrine of chapter 1: the power that deludes the world is the power that gives knowledge when asked (12.37), and fortune and misfortune, creation and dissolution, are all hers (12.38–40). Reading the ‘enemies’ of 12.15 as inner passions is a modern reflection, not the verse’s literal sense.
themes: The Devī’s own phalaśruti: reciting, hearing, remembering
One hearing outweighs a year of offerings
The gods restored, the remnant in Pātāla
Eternal, yet arising again and again
Delusion and knowledge, Lakṣmī and Alakṣmī: one power

conclusion.narrative: Before she leaves, the Goddess tells the gods what the story of her deeds will do for those who keep it. Whoever praises her with these hymns, recites the three stories or hears them on the sacred days is freed from sin, poverty, fear, pestilence, evil dreams and the malice of spirits; where it is recited she is present; one hearing pleases her as much as a year of costly worship; and anyone who remembers her story in fire, flood, prison, battle or pain is set free. Then she vanishes before their eyes. The gods take back their offices and their shares of the sacrifice, and the surviving Daityas withdraw to Pātāla. Medhas gives the king the meaning of everything he has heard: the eternal Goddess comes forth again and again to protect the world; she deludes it and gives it birth, ends it, creates and sustains it; she is fortune and misfortune; and, praised and worshipped, she gives wealth, children, a mind set on dharma and a good end.

vocabulary.en: the praise of the fruits (of recitation): the chapter’s title in the colophon
greatness, glory; here the name of the text itself (12.4, 12.7, 12.14)
hymn of praise; the gods’ and others’ hymns (12.2)
a means of well-being, a rite of blessing (12.7)
presence, nearness: the Devī abiding where her text is recited (12.9; compare सन्निधिकारकम्, 12.20)
a rite of pacification, for averting harm (12.16)
delight, love: what worship and hearing give the Devī (12.11, 12.22)
remembering: the act that saves in danger (12.29; स्मरतः, 12.30)
the great pestilence (12.8); the great Death, her form at dissolution (12.38–39)
misfortune, the opposite of Lakṣmī; also her form in decline (12.40)

constructions: Promises in the future within relative–correlative sentences: यः … स्तोष्यते, तस्य … नाशयिष्यामि (12.2); two relative clauses (ये … कीर्तयिष्यन्ति, 12.3; ये … श्रोष्यन्ति, 12.4) taken up by one correlative (तेषाम्, 12.5).
Gerundives of obligation, with the agent in the instrumental (पठितव्यं समाहितैः, श्रोतव्यम्, 12.7) and a causative pair for reciting and making heard (उच्चार्यं श्राव्यम्, 12.10).
The optative of prescription and of capacity: शृणुयात् ‘one should hear’ (12.16), शमयेत् ‘would quell’ (12.8), मुच्येत ‘would be freed’ (12.29).

Locatives of occasion in series (बलिप्रदाने पूजायाम् अग्निकार्ये महोत्सवे, 12.10; शान्तिकर्मणि … दुःस्वप्नदर्शने … ग्रहपीडासु, 12.16) and locative absolutes (सकृत् सुचरिते श्रुते, 12.22; पतत्सु शस्त्रेषु, 12.28; शुम्भे निहते … निशुम्भे च, 12.34–35).
Ablatives in -तः for sources of fear (शत्रुतः, दस्युतः, राजतः, 12.6), and the ablative with a verb of fleeing (स्मरतः … पलायन्ते, 12.30).
Long sentences across verses: 12.3–5, 12.12–13, 12.20b–22a (the year of worship weighed against one hearing), and 12.25b–29a, a list of perils in apposition to नरः closed by स्मरन् … मुच्येत.
सा एव repeated in series (12.37, 12.39, 12.40) and antithesis term by term (भवकाले / अभावे, लक्ष्मीः / अलक्ष्मीः, वृद्धिप्रदा / विनाशाय, 12.40).
The genitive absolute of spectators (पश्यताम् एव देवानाम्, 12.33) and a concessive with अपि (नित्या अपि … सम्भूय, 12.36).
insights: The Goddess vouches for her own text: the phalaśruti is spoken in her voice, and its condition is attention and devotion — समाहितः, भक्त्या, एकचेतसः (12.2, 12.4, 12.7) — not learning.
Worship is accepted for love, not for correctness: she takes what is offered knowingly or unknowingly (12.11), and one hearing of her story gives her the delight of a year of offerings (12.20–22).
Remembrance is the last refuge: in fire, captivity, storm, battle and pain, where no rite is possible, the one who remembers her story is freed (12.25–30).
Manifestation is her way of protecting: eternal, she comes forth again and again (12.36), and withdraws when the work is done (12.33) — the pattern of all three stories.
One power binds and frees: she deludes the universe and gives knowledge when asked (12.37), returning to Medhas’s first teaching (1.55–57).
Nothing is outside her: dissolution, creation and preservation (12.39), Lakṣmī and Alakṣmī (12.40) are all her forms.
conclusion.srividya: The chapter shares names with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa), noted on the verses: for the promised fruits पापनाशिनी (167) and सर्वापद्विनिवारिणी (913, 12.5), भयापहा (121, 12.6), स्वस्तिमती (448, 12.7) and सर्वव्याधिप्रशमनी (551, 12.8); for the Goddess herself चण्डिका (755) and भगवती (279, 12.32), नित्या (136, 12.36), मोहिनी (562) and वियदादिजगत्प्रसूः (550, 12.37), महाकाली (751, 12.38), and the triad सृष्टिकर्त्री (264), गोप्त्री (266), संहारिणी (268) with अजा (866, 12.39). These are shared Śākta names and ideas, not evidence that one text depends on the other. The chapter states no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine, and its dhyāna in the Gita Press pāṭha is of Durgā, not of a Śrīvidyā form.

key_verses.why: Whoever praises me daily with these hymns, with a collected mind — every affliction of his I will destroy, without doubt.
Freed from every affliction, endowed with wealth, grain and sons, a man will be so by my grace — the line recited on its own as a sampuṭa (variant in GRETIL and Freund).
The delight a year of offerings gives me, a single hearing of this story gives too; heard, it takes away sins and grants health.
Remembering this story of mine, a man is freed from danger; by my power lions, robbers and enemies (flee, 12.30).
Though eternal, the Blessed Goddess comes forth again and again, O king, to protect the world.
By her the universe is deluded and by her it is born; entreated, she grants knowledge; pleased, prosperity.
She alone is the great Death in its time; she, the unborn, becomes creation; she, the eternal, sustains beings.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi throughout: -aḥ → -o before voiced sounds (शत्रुतो न, 12.6; नरो मुच्येत, 12.29; आघूर्णितो वा, 12.27); visarga → ś/s before c/t (स्तवैश्च, 12.2; ग्रहपीडाश्च, 12.17; कृतास्तास्तु, 12.25; वैरिणस्तथा, 12.29); visarga after other vowels → r before voiced sounds (प्रीतिर्मे, 12.22; नृभिर्दृष्टम्, 12.17; सृष्टिर्भवति, 12.39; चक्रुर्विनिहतारयः, 12.34); and visarga kept before a sibilant (रिपवः संक्षयम्, 12.15; उपसर्गाः शमम्, 12.17).

Final t → n before a nasal (तस्मान्मम, 12.7; शमयेन्मम, 12.8; शृणुयान्मम, 12.16; यन्मे, 12.23), → c before c (एतच्चरितम्, 12.10), voiced before voiced sounds (तद्वद् वधम्, 12.3; पठनादेव, 12.19; दूरादेव, 12.30); n + ś → ñch (तस्मिञ्छ्रुते, 12.24); n → ṃs/ṃś before t/c (उपसर्गानशेषांस्तु, 12.8; पुत्रांश्च, 12.41); k → ṅ before n (सम्यङ् नित्यम्, 12.9).

Pūrvarūpa with avagraha (तेऽपि, 12.33; बन्धगतोऽपि, 12.27; वेदनाभ्यर्दितोऽपि, 12.28; महोग्रेऽतुलविक्रमे, 12.35); the print also marks some savarṇa-dīrgha junctions with avagraha (जानताऽजानता, 12.11; तथाऽऽरोग्यम्, 12.22; तथाऽलक्ष्मीः, 12.40).
One declared hiatus: तुष्टा | ऋद्धिम् (12.37), required by the metre.
samasa: Dvandvas for the lists of the phalaśruti: itaretara (शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः, 12.3; रक्षोभूतपिशाचानाम्, 12.19; पशुपुष्पार्घ्यधूपैः, गन्धदीपैः, 12.20) and samāhāra (शस्त्रानलतोयौघात्, 12.6; अहर्निशम्, 12.21), and dvandvas nested in tatpuruṣas (मधुकैटभनाशम्, 12.3; धनधान्यसुतान्वितः, 12.13; सिंहव्याघ्रानुयातः, 12.26).

Tatpuruṣas with participles for the states of the hearer: tṛtīyā (भक्तिसमन्वितः, 12.12; सर्वाबाधाविनिर्मुक्तः, 12.13; दावाग्निपरिवारितः, 12.25; वेदनाभ्यर्दितः, 12.28), dvitīyā (बन्धगतः, 12.27), pañcamī (दुष्कृतोत्थाः, 12.5), caturthī (शान्तिकर्मणि, 12.16), saptamī (वह्निहोमम्, 12.11; वनहस्तिभिः, 12.26).

Agent compounds for the text’s effects and the actors: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas in -कारक (शान्तिकारकम्, 12.18; सन्निधिकारकम्, 12.20) and upapada tatpuruṣas (बलहानिकरम्, 12.19; यज्ञभागभुजः, 12.34; जगद्विध्वंसिनि, 12.35; भूप, 12.36; वृद्धिप्रदा, 12.40).

Prādi and nañ compounds of good and ill (दुष्कृतम्, 12.5; दुःस्वप्नम्, सुस्वप्नम्, 12.17; सुचरिते, 12.22; अलक्ष्मीः, 12.40), an avyayībhāva (असंशयम्, 12.2), bahuvrīhis of state and epithet (एकचेतसः, 12.4; निर्भयः, 12.14; चण्डविक्रमा, 12.32; निरातङ्काः, 12.33; विनिहतारयः, 12.34; अतुलविक्रमे, महावीर्ये, 12.35; महामारीस्वरूपया, 12.38), and karmadhārayas of the divine names (महाकाल्या, 12.38; महामारी, 12.39).
grammar_notes: Epic (ārṣa) forms are kept and explained, not corrected: the future प्रतीच्छिष्यामि on the present stem इच्छ- (12.11), ātmanepada नन्दते (12.15), the nominative उत्पत्तयः as object of श्रुत्वा (12.14), and the neuter दुःस्वप्नम् / सुस्वप्नम् (12.17).
वार्षिकी (12.12) is read as ‘annual’ (from वर्ष ‘year’), not ‘of the rainy season’; प्रसूयते (12.37) as the active ātmanepada of the divādi root, not a passive.
स्मरतः (12.30) is read as the ablative with a verb of fleeing; a genitive is possible. महाकाले (12.38) is taken with महामारीस्वरूपया; it could go with व्याप्तम्.
The three epithets of 12.35a are taken with तस्मिन् = Śumbha, resuming 12.34; grammatically they could qualify निशुम्भे.
12.30 and 12.32 are half-ślokas (ardha) counted as mantras of their own, as the colophon count requires; the ॐ of 12.1 and 12.41 is the pāṭha’s bīja, not part of the verse.
themes: The Devī’s phalaśruti in her own voice
The restoration of the gods and the end of the third story
The eternal Goddess who arises again and again
uncertain: 12.7: स्वस्त्ययनं हि तत् (Gita Press) / स्वस्त्ययनं महत् (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the sense is hardly affected.
12.13: धनधान्यसुतान्वितः (Gita Press) / धनधान्यसमन्वितः (GRETIL, Freund, without ‘sons’) — Textual Verification Required.
12.33: पश्यतामेव देवानां (Gita Press) / पश्यतां सर्वदेवानां (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the sense is the same.
12.35: जगद्विध्वंसिनि (Gita Press) / जगद्विध्वंसके (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the variant gives the regular anuṣṭubh cadence, the Gita Press reading a light sixth syllable.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading itself, are flagged on 12.11 (तथा कृताम्: ‘performed thus’ or ‘likewise performed’), 12.12 (वार्षिकी), 12.14 (nominative उत्पत्तयः), 12.17 (neuter दुःस्वप्नम्), 12.21 (या as the relative of प्रीतिः in 12.22) and 12.35 (the referent of the epithets); 12.7, 12.13, 12.33 and 12.35 carry the variants above.
